title: The Revival, the remembrance of death
hookLine: the final book prepares the soul for meeting its Lord
tomorrow: Dadi hands Amira a tiny, worn book. what's inside?

cards: Sunday afternoon, tea on the table, and a grandmother says, in the same voice she uses for grocery lists: when I die, keep it simple. A plain white cloth. Bury me quickly.
Ask someone to read Ya-Sin. Her granddaughter goes cold. Why would anyone talk about her own funeral so calmly, like it's a trip she's packing for?
Because, in a way, she is. Al-Ghazali ends the Revival, his whole enormous work, with a book on remembering death and what comes after. He put it last, where the whole work ends up.

teach.h: EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.
teach.b: The Qur'an says it simply, in Pickthall's words: "Every soul will taste of death."

And a hadith in at-Tirmidhi has the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, urging people to remember often the thing that cuts pleasures short. That sounds grim until you see what al-Ghazali does with it.
He describes three people remembering death. The first is wrapped up in the world, and remembers death only with dislike, as the thief of everything they have.
The second has turned back to God, and remembers death to get ready: to mend, to forgive, to finish what matters.
The third knows God, and remembers death with something like longing, because it's the meeting with the One they love.
There's a hadith in al-Bukhari that sits right underneath this: whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet them. So the remembrance of death isn't meant to frighten.
It's meant to sort. Ask what you'd do with a day if you remembered it would end, and the trivial things fall off the table. The arguments that don't matter.
The grudges. The phone at dinner.
And here's what makes this a book for living: preparing to meet God, in al-Ghazali's telling, is mostly done on ordinary days, with ordinary people, long before the end.

how: Muslims remember death in prayer and at funerals, which are kept simple, with a plain white shroud and prompt burial; some read al-Ghazali's book on the remembrance of death, the last book of the Revival.

o: al-Ghazali's great work, ending with remembering death
a vigil kept on the anniversary of a death
a funeral prayer said at the graveside by family

games.q: the last book — tap the pairs.

s: al-Ghazali's book on death is meant to frighten people into obedience
it's meant to sort the day: to mend, forgive and finish what matters, and for some, to long for the meeting.
the remembrance of death is the last book of the Revival
he put it last, where the whole work ends up.
for al-Ghazali, preparing to meet God happens mostly at the very end
it's done on ordinary days, with ordinary people, long before.

games.q: you and your brother haven't spoken properly in weeks over something small. you remember today's book. what fits it?
o: send the message that mends it; this is what the remembrance sorts out.
wait for him to apologize first; there's plenty of time.
stay away from him for good so the fight can't grow.
games.why: the second person in al-Ghazali's book remembers death to get ready: to mend, to forgive, to finish what matters. grudges fall off the table.

practice: Write one sentence by hand: what you hope your days were spent on. Then sit calmly with it, breathing slowly.
If this feels too heavy today, set the pen down and simply breathe; and if you are ever in danger, call 988 in the US or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: The Revival, one last time: its final book, on remembering death so the soul is ready to meet its Lord.

orig.note: Arabic: dhikr al-mawt, the remembrance of death, the subject of the Revival's final book.

carryVoice: The line to keep: preparing to meet him, mostly on ordinary days. That closes al-Ghazali, eight days long.
